mcqs.q: On a little-endian x86-64 machine, `uint32_t x = 0x0A0B0C0D;` is stored in memory. What is the value of the **first byte** at `&x` (lowest address)?
options: It is unspecified
mcqs.explanation: Little-endian stores the least-significant byte at the lowest address, so `*(uint8_t*)&x == 0x0D`. Big-endian would put `0x0A` first.

mcqs.q: Which expression correctly tests whether `uint32_t x` is a power of two **for all inputs including 0**?
options: `__builtin_popcount(x) >= 1`
mcqs.explanation: `x & (x-1)` clears the lowest set bit; it is 0 for both powers of two **and** for 0. The leading `x &&` excludes 0. `std::has_single_bit`/`popcount(x)==1` also work.

mcqs.q: For a 64-bit value, which of these is **undefined behaviour**?
options: `x >> 1` for `uint64_t x`
`std::rotl(x, 40)` on a `uint64_t`
mcqs.explanation: `1u` is a 32-bit `unsigned int`; shifting it by 40 (>= its width) is UB. You need `uint64_t{1} << 40` or `1ull << 40`. `std::rotl` is defined at any count (unlike shift), and `>> 1` is fine.

mcqs.q: Under the System V AMD64 calling convention, where does the **third integer argument** arrive and where is a `double` return value placed?
options: `rsi`; returned in `xmm0`
`rdx`; returned in `rax`
`rcx`; returned in `rax`
`rdx`; returned in `xmm0`
mcqs.explanation: Integer args go `rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9`, so the 3rd is `rdx`. Floating-point return values come back in `xmm0` (integer/pointer returns use `rax`).

mcqs.q: Why do compilers emit `xor eax, eax` rather than `mov eax, 0` to zero a register?
options: `xor eax, eax` is a recognized dependency-breaking zeroing idiom that often costs zero execution-port cycles
`mov eax, 0` is undefined behaviour at the ISA level
`xor` zeroes the flags register at the same time, which is required
`xor` is the only instruction that clears the upper 32 bits of `rax`
mcqs.explanation: The renamer recognizes `xor reg, reg` as unconditionally zero, breaks the dependence on the old value, and frees the physical register early. Writing the 32-bit `eax` also zero-extends into `rax` (true for `mov eax, 0` too), so the differentiator is dependency-breaking, not the upper-half clear.

mcqs.q: The unit of transfer between memory and the CPU cache on modern x86 is:
options: A 4 KB page
A 64-byte cache line
A 4096-bit block sized to the L1
A single byte
mcqs.explanation: Caches move fixed 64-byte cache lines, not individual bytes. Reading one `int` pulls in the whole 64-byte line containing it; this is why spatial locality and 64-byte alignment to avoid false sharing matter.

mcqs.q: Why does iterating a `std::list<int>` of N elements typically lose badly to a `std::vector<int>` of the same N, even though both are O(N)?
options: `std::vector` stores ints in registers, `std::list` does not
`std::list` has a worse asymptotic complexity for traversal
Pointer chasing serializes DRAM misses and defeats the hardware prefetcher, while the contiguous vector is prefetched and uses each cache line fully
`std::list::size()` is O(N) so the loop bound is expensive
mcqs.explanation: Each `node = node->next` depends on the load that just completed, so misses serialize at ~100 ns each. A vector is sequential: addresses are known ahead, misses overlap (memory-level parallelism) and the prefetcher front-runs the loop.

mcqs.q: A loop sums a `double` array with a single accumulator and runs ~3x slower than a 4-accumulator version doing the same number of adds. The primary reason is:
options: The compiler refuses to inline the loop
Branch mispredictions on the loop condition
More cache misses in the single-accumulator version
A loop-carried dependency chain limited by FP-add latency, not throughput
mcqs.explanation: Each `s += x[i]` depends on the previous result, one chain paying ~3-4 cycle FP-add latency per step while a second FP-add port sits idle. Independent accumulators expose ILP and approach the throughput limit (~2 adds/cycle).

mcqs.q: What is the value of the expression `-1 < 1u` in C++?
options: `false`
Undefined behaviour
Implementation-defined
`true`
mcqs.explanation: In the usual arithmetic conversions, when a signed and an unsigned operand of equal rank meet, the signed operand converts to unsigned. `-1` becomes `UINT_MAX`, so `-1 < 1u` is `false`. This is the classic sign-conversion trap behind `v.size() > -1` always being false.

mcqs.q: Four x86-64 sequences each leave zero in `eax`: `xor eax, eax`, `mov eax, 0`, `sub eax, eax`, `and eax, 0`. Which is the **odd one out** microarchitecturally?
options: `xor eax, eax`, because it also clobbers flags
`and eax, 0`, because it keeps a true data dependency on the old `eax` and is not a recognized zeroing idiom
`mov eax, 0`, because the immediate makes it slowest
`sub eax, eax`, because subtraction can underflow
mcqs.explanation: `xor`/`sub reg,reg` are dependency-breaking idioms; `mov eax,0` writes a constant independent of the old value. `and eax,0` produces zero but must read the previous `eax` first, chaining onto whatever last wrote it and occupying an ALU port.

coding.prompt: Implement `uint32_t load_be32(const uint8_t* p)` that reads a **big-endian** (network-order) unsigned 32-bit integer from a 4-byte buffer. It must be correct on **any** host — no `reinterpret_cast`, no endianness `#ifdef`. Click **▶ Run tests** to check against the test cases.
hints: The most-significant byte is at `p[0]` for big-endian.
Shift each byte into place and OR them together.
coding.discussion: Never do `*(const uint32_t*)p`: the buffer may be unaligned and the lvalue cast violates strict aliasing — both UB, independent of endianness. Assembling by value is portable and the optimizer still folds it into a single load (plus a `BSWAP` on a little-endian host).

coding.prompt: Write a portable function `uint32_t load_be32(const uint8_t* p)` that reads a **big-endian** 32-bit unsigned integer from a byte buffer, correct on any host (no `reinterpret_cast`, no endianness `#ifdef`).  Click **▶ Run tests** to check against the test cases.
hints: Assemble the value by shifting and OR-ing the bytes.
The most-significant byte is at `p[0]` for big-endian.
Cast each byte to `uint32_t` before shifting so you do not shift an 8-bit value.
coding.discussion: Avoid `*(const uint32_t*)p` and `std::byteswap(*reinterpret_cast<const uint32_t*>(p))` -- those are alignment + strict-aliasing bugs, independent of endianness. If you start from a copied scalar, `std::memcpy` into a local then `ntohl`/`std::byteswap` is also correct. The assemble-by-value form needs no knowledge of host byte order at all.

coding.prompt: Implement `int count_set_bits(uint32_t x)` two ways and explain which the hardware prefers: (a) a portable loop, and (b) the C++20 one-liner that maps to a single instruction.  Click **▶ Run tests** to check against the test cases.
hints: Kernighan's trick `x &= x - 1` removes one set bit per iteration.
C++20 `<bit>` gives `std::popcount`.
`std::popcount` lowers to the `POPCNT` instruction.
coding.discussion: `std::popcount` is `constexpr`, portable, and lowers to `POPCNT` (~3-cycle latency, fully pipelined) -- far better than the loop, whose cost scales with the number of set bits. Prefer `std::popcount` over `__builtin_popcount`; and note `std::countr_zero(0)` is defined (returns width) while `__builtin_ctz(0)` is UB.

hints: A cache line holds 16 ints (64 bytes).
Which loop strides by `N` ints between consecutive accesses?
The fix is to swap the loop nesting order.
coding.discussion: All three do exactly N^2 additions; complexity counts operations, the hardware counts cache lines. The same O(N^2) work is fast or slow purely by whether you stride along cache lines (and let the prefetcher help) or across them. This motivates cache-friendly layouts, blocking/tiling, and SoA in market-data code.

mcqs.q: Processing a *sorted* random array through `if (data[i] >= 128) sum += data[i];` is several times faster than processing the *unsorted* array, even though sorting time is excluded. Why?
options: `std::sort` warms the branch target buffer
Sorting compacts the data so it fits in cache
On the sorted array the data-dependent branch is predictable (long runs of one outcome); on the unsorted array it mispredicts ~50% of the time at ~15-20 cycles each
The compiler vectorizes only sorted arrays
mcqs.explanation: It is about predictability, not presence, of the branch. Sorted data gives long taken/not-taken runs the predictor nails; random data is a coin flip per element. The lesson: make data-dependent branches predictable or remove them.

mcqs.q: When is a `cmov`-based branchless version likely to be **slower** than the equivalent branchy code?
options: When the branch is unpredictable
`cmov` is always faster than a branch
Only when the data does not fit in L1
When the branch is highly predictable, because speculation lets the CPU run past it for free while `cmov` serializes on both inputs
mcqs.explanation: A well-predicted branch is essentially free (the CPU speculates straight through). `cmov` never mispredicts but computes both sides and adds a data dependency (~1-2 cycle latency). So predictable branch -> keep it; unpredictable -> go branchless. Answer: it depends; measure.

mcqs.q: What does the `[[unlikely]]` attribute actually change in the generated code?
options: It changes code layout so the unlikely path is hoisted out of the hot fall-through stream, improving I-cache density; it does not override hardware prediction
It inserts an `lfence` to block speculation
It marks the branch as a `cmov`
It forces the hardware branch predictor to predict not-taken
mcqs.explanation: Hints like `[[unlikely]]`/`__builtin_expect` guide code layout (and inlining), not the runtime predictor's learning. PGO is the systematic version that lays out branches from measured behaviour.

mcqs.q: Under the x86-TSO memory model, which single reordering of memory operations is permitted?
options: StoreStore
StoreLoad (a later load may complete before an earlier store becomes globally visible)
LoadStore
LoadLoad
mcqs.explanation: x86 is Total Store Order: only StoreLoad reordering is allowed, because a store sits in the store buffer before becoming globally visible while a later load can proceed. LoadLoad, StoreStore, and LoadStore stay in program order.

mcqs.q: What does register renaming eliminate?
options: Branch mispredictions
True (read-after-write) data dependencies
False dependencies (write-after-read and write-after-write hazards), by mapping architectural registers onto a larger physical register pool
Cache misses
mcqs.explanation: Renaming removes WAR and WAW false dependencies so independent instructions reusing the same architectural register can execute in parallel. Only true RAW dependencies remain to constrain ordering.

mcqs.q: On x86-64, which `std::atomic` operation requires a real fence instruction (e.g. a `LOCK`-prefixed op or `MFENCE`), making it noticeably more expensive than the others?
options: A relaxed load
An acquire load
A release store
A `seq_cst` store (and any read-modify-write such as `fetch_add`/CAS)
mcqs.explanation: On x86, acquire loads and release stores are plain `MOV`s (only a compiler barrier). A sequentially-consistent store needs a real barrier, and every RMW uses a `LOCK` prefix -- tens of cycles. This is why SPSC rings (release/acquire) crush CAS-heavy MPMC designs.

mcqs.q: Two threads on different cores each write to their own variable, but both variables happen to live in the same 64-byte cache line. The result is a severe slowdown. This is called:
options: False sharing
A capacity miss
A TLB miss
A conflict miss
mcqs.explanation: False sharing: each write invalidates the other core's copy of the shared line, forcing a coherence round-trip per write even though the variables are logically independent. The fix is to pad them onto separate lines (`alignas(std::hardware_destructive_interference_size)`, typically 64 bytes).

mcqs.q: Why do low-latency systems prefer **explicit** huge pages (2 MB/1 GB) over Transparent Huge Pages (THP) for a hot working set?
options: THP pages are smaller than explicit huge pages
Explicit huge pages give deterministic behaviour, whereas THP's background compaction (khugepaged) introduces unpredictable jitter
THP does not reduce TLB misses
Explicit huge pages are always faster to allocate at runtime
mcqs.explanation: Both shrink TLB pressure (one entry covers 512x/262144x more memory). The difference is determinism: THP's asynchronous promotion/compaction perturbs latency, so HFT pre-allocates explicit huge pages instead.

mcqs.q: How many `double`s fit in a single AVX-512 `zmm` register?
mcqs.explanation: A 512-bit register holds 8 doubles (64-bit each) or 16 floats (32-bit each). AVX2 `ymm` (256-bit) holds 4 doubles/8 floats; SSE `xmm` (128-bit) holds 2 doubles/4 floats.

mcqs.q: Under plain `-O2` (no `-ffast-math`), why won't the compiler auto-vectorize a simple `double` summation reduction into one with multiple SIMD accumulators?
options: `-O2` never vectorizes anything
The array is too small to vectorize
SIMD cannot add doubles
Floating-point addition is not associative, so reassociating the sum could change the bit-exact result
mcqs.explanation: Reordering FP adds changes rounding, so the compiler must preserve your association unless you opt in with `-ffast-math`/`-fassociative-math` or `#pragma omp simd reduction`. That trades bit-exact reproducibility for speed -- a real decision in PnL code.

mcqs.q: On Linux with the default first-touch policy, a thread on node 0 `malloc`s a buffer and `memset`s it, then worker threads pinned to node 1 process the second half. Why is this slow?
options: First-touch binds each physical page to the node of the thread that first *writes* it, so the `memset` placed every page on node 0; node-1 workers then make remote accesses across the interconnect
`memset` is not vectorized
The page tables are duplicated per node
`malloc` always allocates on node 1
mcqs.explanation: first-touch places a page on the node whose core first writes it. Initializing the whole buffer on node 0 co-locates everything there, so node-1 workers pay ~1.5-2x remote DRAM latency plus interconnect contention. Fix: first-touch each region from the pinned thread that will own it.

hints: Turn the conditional add into a data dependency, not control flow.
Build a mask that is all-zeros or all-ones from the comparison.
`-(long)(cond)` gives `0` or `-1` (all ones).
coding.discussion: The comparison result becomes a mask and the conditional add becomes pure arithmetic, so there is no control-flow branch to mispredict. The compiler may also achieve this with `cmov`. Note this is a win only because the branch is unpredictable; a highly predictable branch would beat the branchless form because the CPU speculates through it for free. Always measure with `perf stat -e branches,branch-misses`.

coding.prompt:
Two worker threads each repeatedly increment their own counter, but the counters share a cache line and the program is far slower than expected. Fix the false sharing without changing the logic.

```cpp
struct Counters { std::atomic<long> a; std::atomic<long> b; };
```  Click **▶ Run tests** to check against the test cases.
hints: The two atomics sit within one 64-byte cache line.
Use the C++17 portable constant for cache-line spacing.
Pad each counter onto its own line.
coding.discussion: `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size` (typically 64, sometimes 128 on Intel due to adjacent-line prefetch) is the minimum spacing that guarantees `a` and `b` land on different cache lines. Now each thread's write no longer invalidates the other core's line, eliminating the coherence ping-pong. This same padding is mandatory between the head and tail indices of an SPSC ring.

hints: Aliasing between `a` and `b` blocks reordering, CSE, and vectorization.
`__restrict` promises the pointers do not overlap.
Reductions still need `-ffast-math` or a pragma to reassociate, but non-aliasing is the first blocker.
coding.discussion: `__restrict` tells the compiler `a` and `b` never alias, unblocking the load/store reordering vectorization needs. Even then, summing into one `float` is a loop-carried FP dependency that strict IEEE rules forbid reassociating; `-ffast-math` or `#pragma omp simd reduction(+:s)` lets the compiler use multiple SIMD accumulators -- at the cost of bit-exact reproducibility. Verify with `-fopt-info-vec`/`-fopt-info-vec-missed`.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is **private to each thread** rather than shared across threads of the same process?
options: Open file descriptors
The stack (and registers / `thread_local` storage)
Global and static variables
The heap
mcqs.explanation: Threads share the address space: code, globals/BSS, heap, and the file-descriptor table. Each thread privatizes its own stack, registers/instruction pointer, `thread_local` storage, and `errno`.

mcqs.q: A thread calls `getpid()`. Which is true?
options: It causes a context switch but not a mode switch
It always causes a context switch and a mode switch
It causes a mode switch (user->kernel->user) but not necessarily a context switch
It causes neither, because `getpid` runs entirely in user mode
mcqs.explanation: A system call always involves a mode switch (privilege transition, same thread keeps running). A context switch -- the kernel running a *different* thread -- only happens if the call blocks or the thread is preempted. A trivial non-blocking syscall is just a mode switch.

mcqs.q: How can `clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)` return a high-resolution timestamp without ever executing a `syscall` instruction?
options: The CPU caches the last syscall result
It is implemented purely with `rdtsc` and never needs the kernel's value
It uses an `int 0x80` software interrupt instead
It is served from the vDSO: the kernel maps a shared timekeeping page into every process and the call reads it entirely in user mode
mcqs.explanation: The vDSO (virtual dynamic shared object) is a kernel-mapped shared library containing user-mode implementations of `clock_gettime`/`gettimeofday`/`getcpu`. It reads a kernel-maintained shared page with no ring transition, turning a ~hundreds-of-ns trap into a ~tens-of-ns call.

mcqs.q: Why is switching between two threads of the **same process** cheaper than switching between two **different processes**?
options: A different-process switch reloads `CR3` (the page-table base), which invalidates the TLB (absent PCID) and forces costly page walks afterward
Same-process switches skip the scheduler entirely
Different processes always run at a lower priority
Same-process threads share registers, so fewer registers must be saved
mcqs.explanation: Same-process thread switches keep the address space, so `CR3` and the TLB stay warm. A process switch reloads `CR3`, invalidating the TLB (mitigated but complicated by PCID/KPTI) and leaving the resumed task running on cold caches.

mcqs.q: After a successful `fork()`, what does the return value tell each process?
options: Both processes receive `0`
The parent receives the child's PID (>0); the child receives `0`
The parent receives `0`; the child receives the parent's PID
Both receive the child PID
mcqs.explanation: `fork()` returns the child's PID to the parent, `0` to the child, and `-1` on failure. This is how a single code path distinguishes which process it is running in.

mcqs.q: A child process has terminated but its parent has not yet called `wait`/`waitpid`. What is the child's state?
options: It has been fully removed from the process table
Orphan, reparented to PID 1
Zombie: dead-but-unreaped, holding only a process-table slot with its exit status
Sleeping (S)
mcqs.explanation: A terminated, unreaped child is a zombie (`Z`): the kernel keeps a minimal record (exit status) until the parent reaps it. An *orphan* is different -- a still-running child whose parent died, reparented to init/PID 1, which reaps it.

mcqs.q: Which best describes a **major** page fault versus a **minor** page fault?
options: Both require disk I/O; the difference is page size
Minor faults occur only in kernel mode
Major faults are satisfied from RAM/page cache; minor faults read from disk
Minor faults need no disk I/O (allocate+zero a frame or map a cached page, ~single-digit us); major faults require disk I/O (swap-in/file read, ~hundreds of us to ms)
mcqs.explanation: A minor fault is resolved without disk (fresh zeroed frame, or a page already in the page cache). A major fault must fetch from storage and is orders of magnitude slower -- catastrophic on a hot path, which is why HFT pre-faults and `mlock`s its arenas.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes a microkernel from Linux's monolithic design?
options: A microkernel runs device drivers and filesystems as user-space servers, keeping only minimal services (scheduling, IPC, basic MM) in ring 0
A microkernel runs everything in ring 0 for speed
A monolithic kernel cannot load modules at runtime
A microkernel has no system calls
mcqs.explanation: A microkernel keeps the kernel minimal and pushes drivers/FS/networking into user-space servers for strong isolation, at the cost of IPC overhead. Linux is monolithic (all subsystems in kernel space, fast direct calls) but modular (runtime-loadable modules).

mcqs.q: Two `SCHED_FIFO` threads at the **same** real-time priority are both runnable on one core. What happens?
options: They round-robin on a time quantum
The running one keeps the core until it blocks, yields, or a higher-priority RT task preempts it -- same-priority FIFO tasks do not round-robin
The scheduler picks fairly by `vruntime`
Both run simultaneously via hyper-threading
mcqs.explanation: `SCHED_FIFO` has no time slice; a running task holds the CPU until it blocks/yields or is preempted by a strictly higher-priority RT task. `SCHED_RR` is the variant where same-priority tasks round-robin on a quantum.

mcqs.q: What makes a Linux futex ("fast userspace mutex") fast in the uncontended case?
options: It disables interrupts during the lock
It always traps into the kernel but uses a faster code path
The uncontended fast path is a pure userspace atomic CAS on an `int` (~tens of cycles, no syscall); only the contended slow path calls `futex(FUTEX_WAIT)` to park the thread
It spins forever instead of sleeping
mcqs.explanation: The uncontended path flips the lock word with an atomic CAS entirely in user space -- no syscall. Only when there is contention does it call into the kernel (`FUTEX_WAIT`/`FUTEX_WAKE`) to park and wake threads.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the four Coffman conditions required for deadlock?
options: Circular wait
Mutual exclusion
Hold-and-wait
Priority inheritance
mcqs.explanation: The four Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait; breaking any one prevents deadlock. Priority inheritance is a *fix* for priority inversion, not a deadlock condition.

mcqs.q: Two threads acquire `mutex_a` and `mutex_b` in opposite orders and occasionally deadlock. Which standard tool acquires both at once using a deadlock-avoidance algorithm so the lock order no longer matters?
options: `std::scoped_lock(mutex_a, mutex_b)` (built on `std::lock`)
A `std::recursive_mutex`
`std::call_once`
`std::lock_guard` on each mutex separately
mcqs.explanation: `std::scoped_lock` (using `std::lock`'s try/back-off algorithm) locks all supplied mutexes atomically, breaking the hold-and-wait/circular-wait pattern regardless of argument order. Locking each separately with `lock_guard` is exactly what produces the AB-BA deadlock.

coding.prompt: Write a function `int run(const char* path, char* const argv[])` that uses `fork`/`execv`/`waitpid` to run a program, wait for it, and return its exit code (or -1 on failure). Use `_exit` in the child after a failed `exec`, and decode the status with the standard macros.  Click **▶ Run tests** to check against the test cases.
hints: `fork()` returns 0 in the child, the child PID in the parent.
On a successful `exec` the call never returns.
Use `WIFEXITED` / `WEXITSTATUS` to decode `waitpid`'s status.
coding.discussion: The child uses `_exit` (not `exit`) so it does not flush stdio buffers the parent set up. `waitpid` reaps the child (preventing a zombie) and `WIFEXITED`/`WEXITSTATUS` decode the packed status word. A robust supervisor of many children typically reaps in a `SIGCHLD` handler with `waitpid(-1, &status, WNOHANG)` in a loop. Note `fork`'s cost scales with mapped memory because the kernel duplicates page tables -- never fork on a hot path or from a process mapping many GB.

coding.prompt: Implement a thread-safe bounded buffer's `pop()` using a `std::mutex` and a `std::condition_variable`, correctly handling spurious and lost wakeups. Assume members `std::queue<int> q_; std::mutex m_; std::condition_variable cv_;`.  Click **▶ Run tests** to check against the test cases.
hints: Always hold the mutex when changing the predicate and signalling.
Re-check the predicate in a loop, never a bare `if`.
The `wait(lock, pred)` overload atomically releases the lock and waits, closing the lost-wakeup race.
coding.discussion: The predicate-form `wait(lock, pred)` is equivalent to `while (!pred()) cv_.wait(lock);` -- it releases the mutex and blocks atomically, defeating the lost-wakeup race (producer pushes+signals between a manual check and sleep), and the loop absorbs spurious wakeups. The producer must hold the mutex while mutating the queue, then signal. Note this is a control-plane pattern; an HFT hot path would instead busy-poll a lock-free SPSC ring.

mcqs.q: The TCP/IP model has four layers. Which lists the data-unit names from transport down to link, in order?
options: frame -> packet -> segment
segment/datagram (transport) -> packet (internet) -> frame (link)
packet -> frame -> segment
datagram -> frame -> segment
mcqs.explanation: Transport produces a TCP *segment* or UDP *datagram*; the internet layer wraps it in an IP *packet*; the link layer wraps that in an Ethernet *frame*. IP is the 'narrow waist' all layers pass through.

mcqs.q: On a 1500-byte Ethernet MTU, the typical TCP MSS negotiated in the handshake is:
options: 576 bytes
1500 bytes
1460 bytes (1500 - 20 IP header - 20 TCP header)
1472 bytes (1500 - 20 IP - 8 UDP)
mcqs.explanation: MSS is the payload that fits without IP fragmentation: 1500 - 20 (IPv4 header) - 20 (TCP header) = 1460 bytes. 1472 is the analogous figure for UDP (8-byte UDP header).

mcqs.q: What does a router do to the IPv4 **TTL** field, and what does it recompute as a result?
options: Leaves TTL unchanged; recomputes nothing
Decrements TTL; recomputes the Ethernet FCS only
Increments TTL; recomputes the TCP checksum
Decrements TTL by 1 (dropping the packet at 0); recomputes the IPv4 header checksum
mcqs.explanation: Each hop decrements TTL by 1 and drops the packet (returning ICMP time-exceeded) at 0. Because TTL changed, every router must recompute the 16-bit IPv4 header checksum (which covers the header only, not the payload). IPv6 dropped the header checksum to avoid this per-hop work.

mcqs.q: In the IPv4 header, the Protocol field value 17 indicates the payload is which transport protocol?
options: UDP
IGMP
TCP
ICMP
mcqs.explanation: Protocol 17 = UDP, 6 = TCP, 1 = ICMP, 2 = IGMP. The receiving host's internet layer uses this field to demultiplex the payload to the correct transport.

mcqs.q: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) is used to:
options: Map a domain name to an IP address
Resolve an IP address to a link-layer MAC address, using broadcast requests and unicast replies
Decrement TTL at each hop
Negotiate the TCP window size
mcqs.explanation: ARP bridges IP to MAC. It runs directly over Ethernet (EtherType 0x0806), broadcasts the request ('who has this IP?'), receives a unicast reply, and caches the result in the ARP cache. (Name->IP is DNS, a different mechanism.)

mcqs.q: What uniquely identifies a single TCP connection on a host?
options: The IP Identification field
The destination port alone
The 4-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port)
The source MAC address
mcqs.explanation: A TCP connection is keyed by the 4-tuple. This is why one server port can serve many simultaneous clients -- each connection differs in the remote IP/port. The transport demuxes incoming data to the matching socket by this tuple.

mcqs.q: Why do many market-data feeds use UDP rather than TCP, while order-entry uses TCP?
options: UDP is encrypted by default and TCP is not
TCP cannot carry binary data
UDP has a larger header so carries more data

TCP's in-order delivery causes head-of-line blocking -- a lost segment stalls later ones for >= 1 RTT, delivering stale prices -- whereas UDP datagrams are independent and support multicast fan-out; orders need TCP's reliability/ordering
mcqs.explanation: For prices you want the freshest data, not a retransmit of a stale one, and multicast lets one send reach thousands of subscribers; UDP gives both with no head-of-line blocking. Orders cannot be silently lost or reordered, so they use TCP.

mcqs.q: How large is the UDP header, and which statement about message boundaries is correct?
options: 8 bytes; one `sendto` produces exactly one datagram and one `recvfrom` returns exactly one datagram (boundaries preserved)
8 bytes; UDP coalesces datagrams like a byte stream
12 bytes; boundaries are preserved
20 bytes; UDP does not preserve message boundaries
mcqs.explanation: The UDP header is a fixed 8 bytes (source port, dest port, length, checksum). UDP is message-oriented: each `sendto` is one datagram and each `recvfrom` returns exactly one (truncated and lost if the buffer is too small). TCP is the byte stream that does not preserve boundaries.

mcqs.q: The combination of Nagle's algorithm and delayed ACKs can produce a characteristic ~40 ms stall on small messages. Which one-line fix is standard on an order-entry socket?
options: Enable `SO_REUSEADDR`
Set `TCP_NODELAY` to disable Nagle's algorithm
Increase `SO_RCVBUF`
Set the socket to non-blocking
mcqs.explanation: Nagle withholds a small send while unacked data is in flight; delayed ACK withholds the ACK hoping to piggyback -- together they deadlock for ~40 ms. `setsockopt(fd, IPPROTO_TCP, TCP_NODELAY, &one, sizeof one)` disables Nagle and is set on every latency-sensitive TCP session.

mcqs.q: Roughly how much latency does the TCP 3-way handshake add before the first byte of application data can flow?
options: Two full RTTs
Zero -- data flows with the SYN
About one round-trip time (RTT): SYN, SYN+ACK, then the client's ACK precedes data
About 40 ms regardless of RTT
mcqs.explanation: SYN -> SYN+ACK -> ACK costs ~1 RTT before data. Slow start then ramps the congestion window over several more RTTs. This is why HFT pre-establishes and warms connections so a hot order never pays the handshake or slow-start.

coding.prompt: Write a function that opens a UDP socket, allows multiple binders with `SO_REUSEADDR`, binds to a port on all interfaces, and joins an IPv4 multicast group on a specific local interface. Return the socket fd or -1. Signature: `int join_multicast(const char* group, const char* iface_ip, uint16_t port);`  Click **▶ Run tests** to check against the test cases.
hints: Use `socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM, 0)`.
Set `SO_REUSEADDR` before `bind`.
Fill an `ip_mreq` with the group IP and the interface IP, then `setsockopt(IP_ADD_MEMBERSHIP)`.
coding.discussion: `SO_REUSEADDR` lets several consumers bind the same group:port. The interface IP in `ip_mreq` is critical on a multi-homed colo box receiving the A feed on one NIC and the B feed on another -- joining on the wrong interface silently receives nothing. Ports/addresses go on the wire big-endian, hence `htons`/`htonl`. To survive microbursts, size `SO_RCVBUF` and drain quickly (e.g. `recvmmsg`), since the kernel silently drops datagrams when the per-socket queue fills.

coding.prompt: TCP is a byte stream with no message boundaries, so a single `recv` may return a partial or coalesced message. Write `bool recv_exact(int fd, void* buf, size_t n)` that reads exactly `n` bytes (handling short reads and `EINTR`), returning false on EOF or error.  Click **▶ Run tests** to check against the test cases.
hints: Loop until all `n` bytes are read.
`recv` returning 0 means the peer closed (EOF).
Retry on `errno == EINTR`; advance the buffer pointer by bytes received.
coding.discussion: Because TCP does not preserve message boundaries, applications must frame messages themselves (a length prefix or delimiter) and read until they have a whole message -- `recv_exact` is the building block. A single `recv` can return any prefix of the bytes the peer sent, or bytes from several sends coalesced. `recv` returning 0 is EOF (orderly close); negative with `EINTR` should be retried. On a non-blocking socket you would also handle `EAGAIN`/`EWOULDBLOCK` by waiting for readability via epoll.

mcqs.q: On a listening TCP socket, what does `accept()` return?
options: The number of pending connections
The peer's port number
Nothing -- it reuses the listening fd for the new connection
A brand-new file descriptor for the established connection, while the listening fd keeps listening
mcqs.explanation: `accept()` pops a completed-handshake connection off the accept queue and returns a *new* fd for it; the original listening socket continues to accept further connections. Confusing the two fds is a classic bug.

mcqs.q: With **edge-triggered** epoll (`EPOLLET`), what must your code do that level-triggered epoll does not require?
options: Drain the fd in a loop until `recv` returns `EAGAIN`, or data can stall unreported
Call `accept` twice per event
Set `TCP_NODELAY` first
Re-arm the fd with `epoll_ctl` after every event
mcqs.explanation: Edge-triggered mode notifies only on the not-ready -> ready transition, so you must read until `EAGAIN`/`EWOULDBLOCK`; otherwise leftover data sits in the buffer with no further notification. Level-triggered keeps reporting readability as long as data remains.

mcqs.q: On Linux, a `write()` of how many bytes to a pipe is guaranteed **atomic** (will not interleave with another writer's bytes)?
options: Any size
Up to `PIPE_BUF` (4096 bytes on Linux)
Up to 64 KiB (the default pipe capacity)
Exactly one byte
mcqs.explanation: Writes of <= `PIPE_BUF` (4096 on Linux) are atomic; larger writes may be split and interleaved with other writers. The pipe's total buffer defaults to 64 KiB (tunable via `F_SETPIPE_SZ`), but that is capacity, not the atomicity bound.

mcqs.q: What happens when a process writes to a pipe after all read ends have been closed (default signal disposition)?
options: `write` blocks forever
`write` returns 0
The kernel raises `SIGPIPE`, which terminates the process by default (and `write` would otherwise fail with `EPIPE`)
The data is buffered until a reader appears
mcqs.explanation: Writing to a pipe with no readers raises `SIGPIPE` (default action: terminate). If `SIGPIPE` is ignored/blocked, the `write` fails with `EPIPE`. Conversely, reading after all writers close returns 0 (EOF).

mcqs.q: Which `mmap` flag makes writes visible to other processes mapping the same file, turning `mmap` into an IPC channel?
options: `MAP_ANONYMOUS`
`MAP_POPULATE`
`MAP_PRIVATE`
`MAP_SHARED`
mcqs.explanation: `MAP_SHARED` propagates writes to the backing file and to all other mappers of it -- the basis of shared-memory IPC. `MAP_PRIVATE` is copy-on-write (private to the writer). `MAP_ANONYMOUS` has no file backing; `MAP_POPULATE` just pre-faults.

mcqs.q: What is the correct three-step idiom to create and map a POSIX shared-memory region for IPC?
options: `shm_open("/name", ...)` -> `ftruncate(fd, size)` -> `mmap(..., MAP_SHARED, fd, 0)`
`open` -> `read` -> `write`
`malloc` -> `mlock` -> `shm_open`
`mmap` -> `shm_open` -> `ftruncate`
mcqs.explanation: `shm_open` returns an fd to a tmpfs-backed object in `/dev/shm`; `ftruncate` sizes it (mapping past EOF would raise `SIGBUS`); `mmap(MAP_SHARED)` maps it. The object persists until `shm_unlink`. The mapping outlives the fd, so you may `close(fd)` after mapping.

mcqs.q: Why must you NOT store a `std::string`, `std::vector`, or raw pointer between objects inside a shared-memory region used by two processes?
options: They are too large to fit
Those types hold heap pointers (or virtual-table pointers); each process maps the region at a different virtual address, so absolute pointers are meaningless across processes
tmpfs does not support strings
`shm_open` rejects non-trivial types
mcqs.explanation: Only trivially-copyable/standard-layout data is safe. A `std::string`/`std::vector` stores a pointer into one process's heap, invalid in the other; vtable pointers fail similarly. Use offsets/indices relative to the region base (or Boost.Interprocess `offset_ptr`) and construct in place with placement-new.

mcqs.q: The naive read-file-then-write-to-socket path performs four data movements. Which two does `sendfile(2)` eliminate?
options: The interrupt and the context switch
The two unavoidable DMA transfers (disk->page cache and socket->NIC)
The page-cache->user-buffer copy (from `read`) and the user-buffer->socket-buffer copy (from `write`)
The TCP and IP header constructions
mcqs.explanation: `sendfile` keeps data in the kernel: it removes the two CPU copies through user space (the `read` copy and the `write` copy). The two DMA transfers remain (they are unavoidable); on scatter-gather-DMA hardware the page-cache pages go straight to the NIC.

mcqs.q: A subtle requirement when using `MSG_ZEROCOPY` on a TCP send is:
options: It encrypts the payload before sending
It requires `MAP_HUGETLB`
It always reduces latency for small order messages
Completion is asynchronous -- `send()` returns before transmission finishes, so you must not reuse/free the buffer until a completion arrives on the socket's error queue (`MSG_ERRQUEUE`)
mcqs.explanation: The kernel pins your user pages and DMAs from them, so the bytes must stay valid past `send()`; completion (a `SO_EE_ORIGIN_ZEROCOPY` notification with a matching sequence number) is read from `MSG_ERRQUEUE` via `recvmsg`. It is generally only a win above ~10 KB; for tiny messages the pinning/bookkeeping costs more than just copying.

mcqs.q: In an SPSC ring buffer, the producer publishes a new item by storing the head index with **release** semantics and the consumer reads it with **acquire**. What does this release/acquire pair guarantee?
options: A happens-before edge: once the consumer observes the advanced head (acquire), the payload the producer wrote before the release store is guaranteed visible
That only one thread ever runs
That the operations are sequentially consistent across all cores
That the indices never overflow
mcqs.explanation: Release on the publish store pairs with acquire on the load: seeing the new index implies all writes sequenced before the release (the payload) are visible. Using `relaxed` would let the consumer read the payload slot before it is actually published. SPSC needs no CAS because each index has exactly one writer.

mcqs.q: Why does shared memory beat a pipe or local socket for hot-path IPC latency (tens-to-hundreds of ns vs microseconds)?
options: Shared memory uses a faster syscall per message
After one-time setup it has zero kernel copies, zero syscalls in steady state, and no context switch (a busy-polling reader is always runnable) -- only cache-line transfer cost remains
Shared memory compresses the data
Pipes always go over the network
mcqs.explanation: A pipe/socket pays two copies + a syscall each way + a wakeup (microseconds). Shared memory's producer store and consumer load hit the same physical page, so the only cost is cross-core cache-line coherence (tens of ns). The trade-off: you lose built-in backpressure, framing, and isolation -- you build the protocol (e.g. an SPSC ring) yourself.

coding.prompt: Implement a single-producer/single-consumer lock-free ring buffer `SpscRing<T, Cap>` with `bool try_push(const T&)` and `bool try_pop(T&)`. `Cap` must be a power of two. Use the correct memory orderings and pad head/tail to avoid false sharing. No CAS.  Click **▶ Run tests** to check against the test cases.
hints: Power-of-two capacity lets you mask with `& (Cap - 1)` instead of modulo.
Producer writes only `head_`; consumer writes only `tail_`. Each index has one writer, so no CAS is needed.
Publish with `release`, observe with `acquire`; pad `head_` and `tail_` onto separate cache lines.
coding.discussion: Monotonically increasing indices (masked only when indexing) make `head_ - tail_` the exact count and never confuse full with empty. Each index has a single writer, so plain atomic load/store with release (publish) and acquire (observe) suffices -- no read-modify-write, no retry loop. Padding `head_`/`tail_` onto separate cache lines stops the producer's store to `head_` from invalidating the consumer's line. On x86 these acquire/release ops compile to ordinary `MOV`s, so the dominant cost is the cross-core cache-line coherence traffic, not barriers. The layout is trivially-copyable and works in a `MAP_SHARED` region for cross-process IPC. MPMC would require CAS (and brings the ABA problem).

coding.prompt: Write the producer side that creates a POSIX shared-memory object, sizes it, maps it, and publishes a value to a consumer using an atomic flag. Define a shared layout `struct Shared { std::atomic<int> ready; int value; };` and show the `shm_open`/`ftruncate`/`mmap` sequence with placement-construction and release/acquire publication.  Click **▶ Run tests** to check against the test cases.
hints: Open with `O_CREAT | O_RDWR`; the name starts with `/` and has no other slashes.
`ftruncate` before `mmap`, or stores past EOF raise `SIGBUS`.
Construct the struct in place with placement-new; publish `value` then store `ready` with `memory_order_release`.
coding.discussion: The object lives on tmpfs in `/dev/shm` (RAM-backed, no disk I/O) and persists until `shm_unlink`. `std::atomic<int>` works across processes because atomics act on the memory itself, and the release/acquire pair gives the consumer a happens-before guarantee on `value`. After warm-up this hand-off is tens-to-hundreds of ns -- no kernel copy and no syscall per message -- versus single-digit microseconds for a pipe/socket round trip. Only trivially-copyable types may live in the region (no `std::string`/`std::vector`/raw inter-object pointers, since each process maps at a different address); pad hot fields with `alignas(64)` to avoid false sharing. For mutual exclusion you would use a `pthread_mutex_t` initialized `PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED` (ideally `_ROBUST`).

mcqs.q: What is the difference between 'zero-copy' and 'kernel bypass'?
options: Zero-copy only applies to disk I/O
They are synonyms

Zero-copy removes the CPU `memcpy` between NIC DMA buffers and the application buffer; kernel bypass takes the entire kernel network stack off the data path. Bypass implies zero-copy, but not vice versa
Kernel bypass removes copies; zero-copy removes interrupts
mcqs.explanation: Zero-copy is specifically about eliminating the CPU copy; kernel bypass (DPDK, ef_vi) removes the syscall, the stack, the interrupt/softirq, and the copy. A path can be zero-copy while still going through the kernel (e.g. PACKET_MMAP), so bypass is the stronger property.

mcqs.q: For tiny HFT market-data packets (tens of bytes), why does merely eliminating the data copy 'barely move the needle'?
options: The copy is actually free on modern CPUs
Small packets are never copied
The compiler removes the copy automatically
The copy of tens of bytes is dwarfed by the syscall, interrupt, and protocol-processing overhead
mcqs.explanation: For a few dozen bytes the `memcpy` is almost the cheap part; the syscall transition, the interrupt/softirq, and the stack's per-packet work dominate. To win you must also remove the syscall and the interrupt -- which is why full kernel bypass beats copy-avoidance alone for HFT.

mcqs.q: What is **receive livelock**, the failure mode that NAPI was designed to prevent?
options: At high packet rates the CPU spends nearly all its time in interrupt context, starving the bottom-half packet processing, so usable throughput collapses toward zero
Packets arriving out of order
The NIC running out of descriptors
Two threads deadlocking on a socket lock
mcqs.explanation: Each arriving packet raises an interrupt that preempts processing; past a threshold the core is so busy taking interrupts that it never drains the queue, and throughput collapses. NAPI fixes this: one interrupt disables further RX interrupts and switches to polling the ring up to a budget, re-enabling interrupts only when the ring drains.

mcqs.q: Compared to interrupt-driven delivery, pure busy-polling of the NIC removes which costs?
options: It removes the DMA transfer of the frame
IRQ delivery latency, the context switch into a woken thread, the scheduler decision, and C-state exit -- while keeping the core's caches warm
It removes the need for a network cable
It removes the cache-coherence protocol
mcqs.explanation: A pinned, spinning thread is already running on a hot core, so there is no interrupt, no wakeup/context switch, no scheduler hop, and no deep C-state to climb out of. The cost is a fully consumed core -- acceptable for a few latency-critical flows, not for a 10k-connection server.

mcqs.q: What knob does interrupt coalescing (`ethtool -C rx-usecs/rx-frames`) trade off?
options: TCP vs UDP behaviour
Bandwidth vs encryption
Latency vs throughput -- holding off interrupts until N frames arrive or a timer expires raises throughput but adds per-packet waiting time
CPU count vs memory
mcqs.explanation: Coalescing batches RX interrupts, amortizing interrupt overhead (more throughput) at the cost of extra per-packet delay (more latency). It is a direct latency-vs-throughput dial; latency-sensitive setups minimize it (or bypass interrupts entirely).

mcqs.q: In DPDK, what is a Poll Mode Driver (PMD)?
options: A power-management daemon
A protocol stack for TCP
A kernel module that delivers interrupts faster
A userspace driver that continuously spins reading the NIC's RX ring with no interrupts, pegging its core at 100%
mcqs.explanation: A PMD polls the NIC's descriptor rings from userspace in a tight loop, eliminating interrupts and their latency/jitter. It keeps the core at 100% even with no traffic -- intentional in HFT, trading a core for deterministic low latency.

mcqs.q: Why does DPDK back its packet-buffer pools (mempools) with **hugepages**?
options: They provide stable pinned DMA addresses and let far fewer TLB entries cover the buffer pool (fewer TLB misses), with large physically-contiguous regions
Hugepages make the NIC faster
They are required to compile DPDK
Hugepages are encrypted
mcqs.explanation: Hugepages (2 MB/1 GB) give pinned, contiguous memory the NIC can DMA into with stable physical addresses, and one TLB entry covers vastly more memory, slashing TLB misses on the buffer pool. DPDK is also NUMA-aware so mempools/rings/lcores sit on the NIC's node.

mcqs.q: Which statement about VFIO versus UIO for binding a NIC to userspace is correct?
options: UIO programs the IOMMU to constrain DMA; VFIO does not
VFIO (`vfio-pci`) programs the IOMMU to restrict DMA to allowed memory, making it the safer modern choice; UIO has no such DMA protection
They are identical
VFIO requires no kernel support at all
mcqs.explanation: VFIO uses the IOMMU to confine device DMA to permitted regions; UIO (`igb_uio`, `uio_pci_generic`) is the legacy passthrough with no DMA isolation, so a misbehaving device/app could DMA anywhere. VFIO is preferred on modern systems.

coding.prompt: Sketch the busy-poll receive loop structure DPDK uses (run-to-completion on one lcore): repeatedly burst-receive packets, process them, and free the buffers, with no syscalls or blocking. Use `rte_eth_rx_burst` and show why it is non-blocking. (Pseudocode-level DPDK C is fine.)  Click **▶ Run tests** to check against the test cases.
hints: `rte_eth_rx_burst(port, queue, bufs, BURST)` returns 0..BURST mbuf pointers without blocking.
When it returns 0 you just spin again -- no sleeping.
Free each mbuf with `rte_pktmbuf_free` after processing.
coding.discussion: `rte_eth_rx_burst` is non-blocking: it returns however many frames are ready (0 to BURST) by reading descriptor memory and never traps into the kernel. The hot loop contains no `recv`, no `socket`, no `malloc`, no lock, and no scheduler interaction -- so there is no interrupt latency, no context switch, no C-state wakeup. The trade-off is a core pegged at 100% even with zero traffic, which is correct for HFT: you spend a core to buy deterministic, sub-microsecond, low-jitter delivery. Batching (the `_burst` APIs) amortizes per-packet PCIe/descriptor cost for line-rate throughput. The lcore, its mempool, and rings should all live on the NIC's NUMA node.

mcqs.q: Why is `std::vector::push_back` described as amortized O(1) even though a single call can be O(n)?
options: Each insertion copies only one element
Reallocation never actually happens
Capacity grows geometrically (e.g. x2), so the total reallocation work across n insertions is 1 + 2 + 4 + ... < 2n = O(n), i.e. O(1) per insertion on average
`push_back` is implemented in hardware
mcqs.explanation: A growth reallocation copies all elements (O(n)), but because capacity doubles, those expensive events are geometrically rare; summed over n pushes the total is bounded by 2n, giving O(1) amortized per push.

mcqs.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of a lookup in `std::unordered_map`, and when does it occur?
options: O(1) always, by construction
O(n log n), during a rehash
O(log n), when the tree is unbalanced
O(n), when adversarial keys all hash into a single bucket
mcqs.explanation: `unordered_map` is O(1) average but degrades to O(n) when every key collides into one bucket (worst case / adversarial input). A balanced `std::map` (red-black tree) is O(log n) for lookup in all cases.

mcqs.q: For small n (say a few dozen ints), a linear scan over a contiguous array often beats an O(1) `std::unordered_map` lookup. Why?
options: The contiguous scan benefits from prefetching, vectorization, and no pointer chasing, while the hash map pays cache misses and indirection that dominate at small n
`unordered_map` lookups are O(n^2)
The compiler refuses to optimize hash maps
The array has lower asymptotic complexity
mcqs.explanation: Big-O ignores constants and the cache. A small contiguous array is one or two cache lines the prefetcher loves; the hash map chases pointers and misses cache. Below ~50-1000 elements the linear scan wins despite being O(n) vs O(1).

mcqs.q: What does the compiler's 'as-if' rule permit?
options: Any transformation, even one that changes program output
Any transformation, provided the program's observable behaviour (volatile accesses, I/O, output at termination) is preserved
Only optimizations explicitly listed in the standard
Optimizations only at -O3
mcqs.explanation: The as-if rule lets the compiler reshape code freely as long as observable behaviour is unchanged. Copy elision (RVO) and `-ffast-math` are the notable cases where the compiler is granted extra latitude beyond strict as-if.

mcqs.q: Why is `-ffast-math` unacceptable for pricing/PnL computations?
options: It makes the binary larger
It disables inlining
It permits reassociation of floating-point operations (which is not associative) and assumes no NaNs/Infs, so results can change bit-for-bit and lose reproducibility
It only works at -O0
mcqs.explanation: `-ffast-math` lets the compiler reassociate FP, flush denormals, and assume no NaN/Inf. Since FP addition is not associative, the numeric result can change -- unacceptable where bit-exact, reproducible PnL is required.

mcqs.q: Why does potential pointer **aliasing** block optimizations like vectorization and common-subexpression elimination?
options: Aliasing only affects debug builds
Aliasing disables inlining specifically
Aliased pointers are always null
If two pointers might refer to overlapping memory, the compiler must assume a write through one can change reads through the other, forbidding reordering/caching of those values
mcqs.explanation: When the compiler cannot prove non-overlap, it must conservatively assume any store may affect any later load, killing reordering, CSE, and vectorization. Promising non-overlap with `__restrict` re-enables these optimizations.

mcqs.q: Which best characterizes the cost difference between stack and heap allocation?
options: Stack allocation is roughly a single pointer adjustment (~1 cycle); heap allocation costs tens of ns (warm free list) up to us if it must syscall or page-fault
Heap allocation is always faster because it is cached
Both cost exactly the same
Stack allocation requires a syscall per frame
mcqs.explanation: A stack allocation is essentially bumping the stack pointer (sub-ns). The heap allocator may hit a warm free list (~tens of ns), contend on a lock (hundreds of ns), syscall via brk/mmap (~us), or trigger a first-touch page fault (~us). Keep allocation off the hot path.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes an **arena (monotonic) allocator** from a general-purpose allocator?
options: It can free individual objects in O(1)

It hands out memory by bumping a pointer through one big buffer and can only reset everything at once (no per-object free) -- allocation is a couple of instructions with no free list, lock, or syscall
It always uses mmap per allocation
It is slower but thread-safe
mcqs.explanation: An arena grabs a big buffer once and bump-allocates slices; you cannot free individual objects, only reset the whole arena. That makes allocation near-free and is ideal for per-tick scratch memory. `std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource` provides this.

mcqs.q: What is the fundamental limitation of plain reference counting (as in `std::shared_ptr`)?
options: It fragments the heap badly
It pauses all threads periodically
It cannot reclaim reference cycles (A->B, B->A unreachable but counts never reach zero), and atomic count updates cost in multithreaded code
It requires a separate GC thread
mcqs.explanation: Reference counting reclaims immediately and incrementally (no big pause), but a cycle keeps counts above zero forever and leaks. `std::weak_ptr` breaks cycles manually; CPython adds a separate cycle collector. Atomic increments/decrements also cost ~tens of ns and bounce cache lines.

mcqs.q: The 'weak generational hypothesis' underpinning generational GC states that:
options: Objects never die
Cycles are impossible
Old objects are collected most often
Most objects die young, so a frequently-collected young generation (nursery) reclaims most garbage cheaply, while the old generation is collected rarely
mcqs.explanation: Because most allocations are short-lived, generational collectors collect the small young generation often and cheaply (copying the few survivors) and the large old generation rarely. A write barrier maintains a remembered set of old->young pointers so young collections need not scan the whole old gen.

mcqs.q: In a hot loop, what is usually the **largest** hidden cost of a `virtual` call (beyond the indirection itself)?
options: It is an inlining barrier: the compiler cannot see which function runs, so it cannot inline and loses downstream optimizations (constant propagation, vectorization); megamorphic sites also risk branch mispredictions
Virtual calls allocate heap memory each time
Virtual calls always throw exceptions
The vtable consumes too much memory
mcqs.explanation: The vtable lookup and indirect call are a few extra cycles, and a megamorphic indirect target can mispredict (~15-20 cycles). But the dominant cost is lost inlining and the optimizations it unlocks. Hot paths use static polymorphism (CRTP, templates, `std::variant`) instead.

mcqs.q: If a hot loop reads only the `price` field of records, why can Struct-of-Arrays (SoA) outperform Array-of-Structs (AoS)?
options: SoA uses less total memory
SoA stores all `price` values contiguously, so each 64-byte cache line is full of useful data and the loop vectorizes; AoS drags the cold fields (qty/id/side) into cache on every record
AoS cannot be iterated
SoA avoids the need for a loop
mcqs.explanation: With AoS, fetching one `price` pulls the rest of the record's fields you do not need, wasting bandwidth and cache. SoA keeps `price` dense and contiguous, so you fetch ~8 doubles of useful data per line and the prefetcher/SIMD engine love it -- a core data-oriented-design technique.

coding.prompt: Implement a minimal `ArenaAllocator` for per-tick scratch memory: it bump-allocates aligned slices from a fixed buffer and supports `reset()` to reclaim everything at once. Provide `void* allocate(size_t bytes, size_t align)` and `void reset()`. No per-object free.  Click **▶ Run tests** to check against the test cases.
hints: Track a current offset into the buffer.
Round the offset up to the requested alignment before carving.
`reset()` just sets the offset back to 0.
coding.discussion: Allocation is a couple of instructions -- align the offset, bump it -- with no free list, no lock, and no syscall, so it is far cheaper than a general `malloc`. The trade-off is the defining one: you cannot free a single object, only `reset()` the whole arena, which fits per-tick scratch memory perfectly (allocate freely during the tick, reset at the end). This is exactly the model `std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource` provides; combine it with placement-new (or pmr containers) to construct objects in the arena's bytes. Pre-fault and `mlock` the backing buffer at startup so the hot path never takes a page fault.

coding.prompt: Replace a hot-path `virtual` dispatch with CRTP (static polymorphism) so the dispatched call can inline. Show a `Strategy<Derived>` base whose `run()` forwards to the derived `onTick()`, and a `Momentum` strategy. Explain why this avoids the virtual-call cost.  Click **▶ Run tests** to check against the test cases.
hints: The base is a template parameterized on the derived type.
`run()` does `static_cast<Derived*>(this)->onTick()`.
No `virtual` keyword anywhere -- dispatch is resolved at compile time.
coding.discussion: With CRTP the concrete type is known at compile time, so `run()` -> `onTick()` is a direct call the compiler can inline -- there is no vtable load, no indirect call, and therefore no branch-target misprediction, and (most importantly) no inlining barrier, so constant propagation and vectorization can flow across the call. Use this on hot paths where the strategy type is fixed at compile time. Genuine runtime polymorphism (`virtual`) is appropriate only on cold paths where the type set is unknown until runtime (plugins, config), per the zero-overhead principle: you do not pay for dynamic dispatch you do not need.
